Authors_and_Year: Arne Bewersdorff, Marie Hornberger, Claudia Nerdel, Daniel S. Schiff (2024)
Target_Population_and_Region: Undergraduate and graduate university students | United States, United Kingdom, and Germany
Primary_Objective: To investigate how cognitive (AI literacy), affective (AI interest, attitudes), and behavioral (use of AI) variables build AI self-efficacy among university students, and to identify distinct student profiles to guide tailored educational initiatives.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Not applicable (Focuses on psychological variables related to AI adoption: AI self-efficacy, AI literacy, Interest in AI, and General Attitudes Towards AI).
Digital_Wellbeing_Passive_Indicators: None (The study relies entirely on active, self-reported survey data).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: AI self-efficacy (8-item scale), AI literacy (27 multiple-choice items + 1 sorting item), Interest in AI (5-item modified PISA scale), Positive and negative attitudes towards AI (8-item General Attitudes Towards AI scale), and Use of AI (2 items).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) for unsupervised clustering (profiling students) and Path Analysis (Structural Equation Modeling - SEM) for modeling causal relationships.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: A three-component "VVE" Gaussian Mixture Model was selected as the best fit based on Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). For Path Analysis, the linear model showed excellent fit (e.g., CFI > 1.0, RMSEA = 0.000 for US/Total sample).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / White-box statistical modeling (Path analysis and GMM natively provide interpretability through path coefficients and component means).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations. However, the study provides tailored educational recommendations for three identified student groups ('AI Advocates,' 'Cautious Critics,' and 'Pragmatic Observers').
Actionable_System_Features: Not applicable (The paper focuses on educational policy and curriculum design rather than an automated intervention system).
Main_Strengths: Large, cross-national sample (US, UK, Germany); robust combination of statistical methodologies (Path Analysis and GMM); practical identification of distinct student profiles for targeted education.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design captures data at only a single point in time; sample relies on the Prolific platform which may not be fully representative of all demographics (e.g., socioeconomic status); limited exclusively to Western contexts.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Lack of research in non-Western contexts (including LMICs/Bangladesh); need for longitudinal studies to track the development of AI self-efficacy over time; no utilization of passive digital logging to measure actual AI usage; limited exploration of how socioeconomic status influences socio-cognitive relationships with AI.

Authors_and_Year: Shuo Gong, Yunjing Li, Haijiang Li (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Junior and senior high school students (Adolescents) | China (Five cities: Ningbo, Xinji, Zhengzhou, Hengyang, and Jianli)
Primary_Objective: To examine the multi-level ecological structure of academic burnout in adolescents by combining machine learning with network analysis, identifying key multi-ecological predictors and their structural interrelations.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Student Burnout Inventory (SBI) (adapted for Chinese adolescents, based on the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Student Survey). Depressive symptoms were measured using PHQ-9.
Digital_Wellbeing_Passive_Indicators: None used. (Digital stress measures such as social media online vigilance and smartphone withdrawal were captured entirely via self-report).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 61 variables spanning individual, family, school, and digital domains. Key indicators include academic burnout, depressive symptoms (PHQ9), psychological resilience (PsyRes), subjective happiness, physical aggressive behavior, teacher-student relationships (TSRe), school belonging, academic pressure, parent-child alienation, and digital stress (social media online vigilance, smartphone withdrawal).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, and LightGBM.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: Support Vector Machine (SVM) with an RBF kernel achieved the best overall performance (AUC = 0.830, F1-Score = 0.750, Accuracy = 0.747).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: Kernel SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was used to extract global feature importance and directional effects. RFECV (Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation) was used for feature selection, followed by Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM) network analysis to interpret the structural relationships between the selected features.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations are generated for users directly. The study offers population-level recommendations for school policy and resource allocation.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable system. Recommends implementing a multi-tiered, school-based support framework (e.g., targeted counseling for co-occurring emotional/digital difficulties, digital literacy education, and boundary-setting guidance for those with high online vigilance).
Main_Strengths: Integration of predictive machine learning (SVM) with structural network analysis (GGM) to understand both risk factors and their interconnections; large and geographically diverse sample within China; consideration of multi-ecological factors including the digital domain.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences; reliance on an abbreviated set of items for the burnout measure rather than the full scale; reliance solely on self-reported data subject to reporting bias.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Lack of multi-source and objective behavioral indicators, specifically the absence of passive digital logging to measure true digital behavior; absence of longitudinal studies to capture dynamic risk evolution; need for cross-cultural validation in other settings (e.g., other LMICs like Bangladesh, as the study focuses strictly on China).

Authors_and_Year: Seo-Jun Lee (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Undergraduate university students | Busan, South Korea
Primary_Objective: To examine the relationship between emotional regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, rumination) and academic burnout, and to assess the mediating role of psychological distress.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS) for burnout; Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21) for psychological distress; Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ) and Cognitive Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (CERQ) for regulation strategies.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Emotional regulation strategies (cognitive reappraisal, expressive suppression, acceptance, problem-solving, rumination), academic burnout dimensions (emotional exhaustion, cynicism, academic efficacy), psychological distress (depression, anxiety, stress), and demographic factors (gender, age, year of study).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None (The study relies entirely on traditional inferential statistics, specifically hierarchical multiple regression and bootstrapped mediation analysis).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The final hierarchical regression model explained 35.9% of the total variance in academic burnout scores (ΔR² = 0.312 for emotion regulation strategies specifically).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None/Not Applicable (Uses traditional white-box statistical modeling, such as regression coefficients and mediation pathways).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable system. The paper recommends policy-level interventions such as campus-based emotional regulation training programs (focusing on cognitive reappraisal and problem-solving) and early screening at the start of each semester.
Main_Strengths: Expands beyond the classic reappraisal-suppression dichotomy by including multiple regulation strategies; uses mediation analysis to explain the mechanism via psychological distress; provides empirical evidence from a collectivist cultural context.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal interpretation; sample drawn from a single metropolitan university limits generalizability; exclusive reliance on self-report surveys introduces potential shared-method variance bias.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: No integration of behavioral or physiological indicators (specifically lacking passive digital logging); absence of longitudinal or experience-sampling designs to track temporal ordering; lacks representation of other non-Western contexts such as LMICs (e.g., Bangladesh).

Authors_and_Year: Alireza Dehghan, Negin Ashrafi (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Medical and non-medical university students | Lausanne, Switzerland
Sample_Size: 886 (Primary cohort, 2022) validated against 2,580 longitudinal observations and 701 non-medical students.
Primary_Objective: To audit construct overlap in explainable machine learning (XML) pipelines applied to burnout-depression prediction, demonstrating that apparent cross-population stability in XAI risk hierarchies is largely a psychometric artefact rather than a learned generalisable risk structure.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory–Student Survey (MBI-SS) for burnout; Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) for depression; State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T) for trait anxiety.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 10 demographic and psychological predictors including trait anxiety (STAI-T), health satisfaction, age, academic year, psychotherapy history, partnership status, employment status, weekly study hours, mother tongue, and sex.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Ridge, Lasso, ElasticNet, Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: ElasticNet (L1+L2 regularisation) was selected as the primary model, achieving an R² of 0.414 and MAE of 9.26 on the primary test set.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) via LinearExplainer. Crucially, the study introduces a novel "residualization protocol" to audit SHAP results for construct overlap (i.e., isolating shared variance between correlated variables via regression).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations are generated.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable intervention system. The study strictly concludes that individual-level clinical prediction is currently not actionable using these feature sets due to high uncertainty (conformal prediction intervals averaged 35.4 units on a 100-point scale). It recommends researchers mandate orthogonality checks (residualization) before interpreting feature hierarchies.
Main_Strengths: Exposes a critical methodological flaw in XAI mental health research (construct overlap); introduces a robust, mathematically sound residualization protocol; leverages comprehensive multi-cohort validation (longitudinal and cross-faculty).
Key_Limitations: Data strictly from a single institution (University of Lausanne) limits cross-institutional generalisability; the composite outcome index (BDCI) lacks independent psychometric validation; does not incorporate potentially critical predictors like financial stress or sleep quality.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete absence of physiological data or ecological momentary assessment (passive digital logging); lack of prospective designs testing cross-institutional variations; no exploration of diverse demographics or non-Western/LMIC contexts (e.g., Bangladesh).

Authors_and_Year: Daniel Cristóbal Andrade-Girón, William Joel Marin-Rodriguez, Marcelo Gumercindo Zuñiga-Rojas, Abrahan Cesar Neri-Ayala, Edgar Tito Susanibar-Ramírez, Miguel Angel Aguilar-Luna-Victoria (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: University students | Dharan, Nepal
Primary_Objective: To develop, compare, and validate multiple ensemble machine learning models for multiclass prediction of student stress, utilizing a rigorous evaluation framework and explainable AI (XAI) analysis.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Public "Student Stress Factors" dataset (Kaggle), which aggregates responses to classify a target variable (stress_level) into three ordinal categories: low, medium, and high.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 20 predictor variables across psychological, physiological, social, environmental, and academic domains (e.g., sleep quality, blood pressure, social support, self-esteem, depression, anxiety level, living conditions, headache, extracurricular activities, bullying, academic performance, basic needs, noise level).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Nine ensemble and boosting algorithms for tabular data: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, Extra Trees, Bagging, Voting, Stacking, XGBoost, and LightGBM.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: Gradient Boosting achieved the highest average performance in nested cross-validation (Accuracy: 89.55%, F1-weighted: 89.54%, MCC: 0.845, ROC-AUC weighted: 98.59%). Independent holdout accuracy was 0.8818. (Note: XGBoost and LightGBM showed comparable, statistically equivalent performance).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) for global beeswarm and local waterfall decomposition; LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) for localized probabilistic prediction analysis.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable system. The findings act as a guide for psychoeducational interventions (e.g., sleep hygiene programs, personalized tutoring, academic support), but the authors emphasize that the model requires prospective validation before integration into institutional early warning systems.
Main_Strengths: Highly rigorous machine learning pipeline utilizing nested cross-validation, probabilistic calibration, and nonparametric statistical testing (Friedman test); comprehensive multi-criteria comparison of ensemble families; robust integration of both global and local XAI tools (SHAP and LIME).
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional, observational dataset limits causal inference; treatment of ordinal stress levels as nominal classes ignores proximity information between levels; relies entirely on a single public dataset from one university, limiting generalizability.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Although the study targets an LMIC (Nepal), it lacks external validation across other socio-cultural contexts (e.g., Bangladesh) to prove model transferability; relies exclusively on self-reported survey data without multimodal or objective physiological/behavioral sources (e.g., passive digital logging); lacks longitudinal monitoring to track the incidence of stress over time.

Authors_and_Year: Saima Alam, Mohammad Arif Ul Alam (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Internal medicine resident physicians | United States (Massachusetts)
Sample_Size: 28 (primary clinical dataset); also evaluated on public datasets WESAD (n=15) and SWELL-KW (n=25).
Primary_Objective: To develop and validate EMBRACE, an explainable multitask deep learning framework that predicts and explains future burnout in resident physicians using wearable sensor data and automatic clinical survey completion.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Mini-Z Burnout Survey (a clinically validated 10-item tool assessing burnout, stress, and job satisfaction).
Digital_Wellbeing_Passive_Indicators: Continuous wearable physiological data (heart rate variability, skin conductance/EDA, skin temperature, and 3-axis accelerometry) collected via the Empatica E4 wristband. Workplace behavioral metrics such as sedentary activity duration, time spent on EMR (Electronic Medical Records), and interruption frequency.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Mini-Z survey responses (perceived stress, control over workload, EMR stress, job satisfaction) and self-reported sleep quality.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Adaptive Multitask Deep Learning (CNN + LSTM architecture) using Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) for few-shot domain adaptation. Baselines included Bi-LSTM, Random Forest, Learning Vector Quantization, Gaussian Mixture Models, and Decision Trees.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: EMBRACE (Adaptive Multitask Deep Learning) outperformed baselines. On the primary clinical dataset for burnout prediction, it achieved 94.7% Accuracy, 94.7% Precision, 94.7% Recall, and 95.1% F1-score.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations). SHAP values were used to generate clinical visualizations, including feature importance plots and time-series summaries mapping daily activities to predicted stress levels.
Personalized_Recommendations: Yes. The EMBRACE framework automatically sends an end-of-day email to the resident. This email includes a personalized visual breakdown of their daily workload, burnout predictions, and specific recommendations to mitigate future burnout risks based on their unique SHAP feature importance (e.g., reducing EMR time or managing interruptions).
Actionable_System_Features: Automated end-of-day email alerts, automated completion of the Mini-Z survey to save time, visual daily stress/activity summaries, and a web-based feedback loop for residents/clinicians to validate the model's predictions.
Main_Strengths: Highly innovative integration of passive physiological sensors with multitask deep learning to predict both burnout states and auto-complete clinical surveys; strong focus on clinical trustworthiness via SHAP-based email interventions; validated on both real-world clinical and public datasets.
Key_Limitations: Very small primary clinical sample size (n=28); short data collection window (2 to 7 days per participant); study conducted at a single US hospital, limiting broad generalizability.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Absence of long-term longitudinal studies to evaluate if the email-based interventions actually reduce burnout over months/years; lack of validation in diverse or resource-constrained global health systems (such as LMICs/Bangladesh); potential to include deeper social interaction metrics.

Authors_and_Year: Willian Sierra Barón, Andrés Gómez Acosta, Laura Natalia Calceto Garavito, Hernán David Romero Reyes, Juan David Salazar Salamanca (2025)
Target_Population_and_Region: Undergraduate psychology university students | Colombia (Andean and Amazonian regions)
Primary_Objective: To determine the psychometric properties (validity and reliability) of the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS) in university students from southern Colombia, an area characterized by rurality, socioeconomic precariousness, and armed conflict.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS). The Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-Student Version (UWES-S) was also utilized to assess concurrent and discriminant validity.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Sociodemographic questionnaire (gender, faculty, period of study, socioeconomic level, marital status), MBI-SS dimensions (exhaustion, cynicism, academic efficacy), and UWES-S dimensions (vigor, dedication, absorption).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study strictly employs traditional psychometric validation methods, specifically exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis via Structural Equation Modeling (SEM).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: A 14-item structural equation model (excluding item 15) demonstrated the best fit, explaining 74.76% of the cumulative variance with adequate goodness-of-fit indicators (CFI > .90, RMSEA < .100) and high internal consistency (McDonald's ω = .83).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable (Relies on traditional white-box psychometric statistics and structural equation modeling).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations are provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study recommends using the validated MBI-SS tool to systematically monitor burnout, identify risk profiles in public institutions, and guide the implementation of curricular strategies, tutoring, and mental health services tailored to specific territorial/regional conditions.
Main_Strengths: Expands burnout research to a historically under-researched, vulnerable region in Latin America (southern Colombia); utilizes robust psychometric validation techniques including gender invariance testing; highlights the impact of socio-educational contexts on burnout.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design; purposive/convenience sampling; restricted to undergraduate psychology students, which limits generalizability to other academic disciplines or populations.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete reliance on traditional self-reported surveys with no integration of objective, passive digital logging or behavioral markers; absence of predictive machine learning frameworks to anticipate burnout before it occurs; need for broader longitudinal studies in diverse LMIC contexts outside of Latin America (e.g., Bangladesh).

Authors_and_Year: Liang Zhe Chong, Lee Kien Foo, Sook-Ling Chua (2025)
Target_Population_and_Region: Systematic review covering various student populations (Primary, Secondary/High School, and University students) | Global (Multiple countries reviewed)
Sample_Size: 38 studies included in the systematic review.
Primary_Objective: To systematically review recent literature (2019–2024) investigating the diverse factors contributing to burnout across different student populations and to summarize mitigation strategies.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: The review found that the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) was the most widely used tool (18 papers), followed by the School Burnout Inventory (SBI) (6 papers). Other tools included the Copenhagen Burnout Inventory, Burnout Assessment Tool, and Oldenburg Burnout Inventory.
Digital_Wellbeing_Passive_Indicators: None utilized directly (this is a literature review). However, the review identifies "problematic internet use" and "excessive use of digital teaching technologies" as key risk factors, which were uniformly measured via self-reports in the underlying studies rather than passive logging.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: The review synthesizes predictors into three categories: Environmental Factors (school environment, impact of digital technologies, social/family support), Psychosocial Factors (psychosocial competencies like grit and emotional regulation, coping strategies), and Other Factors (academic performance, demographics, lifestyle choices like sleep and exercise).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The review notes that the field overwhelmingly relies on traditional statistical methods, primarily Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) (13 papers), Linear Regression (10 papers), Logistic Regression (5 papers), and Latent Profile Analysis (4 papers).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: Not applicable (Systematic Review of statistical studies).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic recommendations provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The review recommends policy-level interventions: fostering supportive school environments, teaching healthy internet habits to mitigate digital isolation, building psychosocial competencies (e.g., emotional regulation), and promoting adaptive coping strategies.
Main_Strengths: Provides a highly comprehensive global synthesis of risk and protective factors for student burnout across all educational levels; clearly categorizes variables into environmental, psychosocial, and demographic domains.
Key_Limitations: Limited to articles published between 2019 and 2024; the review's findings are constrained by the methodologies of the primary studies, the vast majority of which are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: The review starkly highlights a methodological gap across the field: the complete reliance on self-report questionnaires (like the MBI) rather than objective behavioral data such as passive digital logging. Furthermore, the absence of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models and explainable AI (XAI) frameworks in the reviewed literature points to a significant gap in creating proactive, technology-driven early warning systems for students.

Authors_and_Year: M. Graça Pereira, Martim Santos, Renata Magalhães, Cláudia Rodrigues, Odete Araújo, Dalila Durães (2025)
Target_Population_and_Region: Undergraduate and graduate psychology students | Northern Portugal
Primary_Objective: To analyze the relationship between psychological and lifestyle variables and academic burnout, and to identify distinct burnout risk profiles among psychology students using machine learning algorithms.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory—Student Survey (MBI-SS).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Psychological well-being (QGBEP), psychological distress (DASS21), difficulties in emotional regulation (DERS), sleep quality (PSQI), physical activity (IPAQ), and dietary inflammatory index (DII) derived from a Food Frequency Questionnaire.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: K-means clustering (for initial risk profiling), Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Machine (SVM) (for supervised classification of the profiles).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: XGBoost achieved the best overall performance with 97.53% Accuracy, 94.73% F1-score, 90.00% Precision, and 99.99% Recall.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Black-box. (While K-means was used to establish descriptive cutoffs for profiles, no formal explainable AI techniques like SHAP or LIME were applied to interpret the supervised ML models).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were generated.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study advocates for a "stepped-care approach" at the institutional level, using the identified variable cutoffs for early screening and implementing psychoeducational programs targeting emotional regulation and healthy lifestyle habits (sleep, anti-inflammatory diet).
Main_Strengths: Extends beyond standard psychological variables by integrating detailed lifestyle factors (specifically the dietary inflammatory index); uses a combination of unsupervised (K-means) and supervised ML to establish data-driven risk profiles.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions (e.g., potential bidirectional relationship between emotional regulation and burnout); small sample size restricted solely to psychology students from a single Portuguese university limits generalizability.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete reliance on self-reported surveys without any objective physiological metrics or passive digital logging (e.g., objective sleep tracking or physical activity logging); lack of longitudinal validation; absence of XAI methods to transparently interpret the ML models; lack of validation in non-Western or LMIC settings (e.g., Bangladesh).

Authors_and_Year: Hanif Abdul Rahman, Madeline Kwicklis, Mohammad Ottom, Areekul Amornsriwatanakul, Khadizah H. Abdul-Mumin, Michael Rosenberg, Ivo D. Dinov (2023)
Target_Population_and_Region: University students | Southeast Asia (ASEAN countries: Brunei Darussalam, Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam)
Primary_Objective: To predict and classify negative mental well-being among university students using machine learning models based on self-reported health-risk behaviors and demographic indicators.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: A multi-site online cross-sectional survey categorizing mental well-being into a binary outcome (positive or negative/poor) alongside non-communicable disease risk factors.
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 20 features including health-risk behaviors (number of sports activities per week, sedentary hours, hours of sleep, fruit/vegetable intake, salt intake, eating snacks/fast food, sugar beverages, alcohol consumption, smoking) and demographic/academic variables (body mass index [BMI], age, gender, grade point average [GPA], living arrangement).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Generalized Linear Model (Logistic Regression), k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN), Naïve Bayes, Neural Networks, Random Forest, Recursive Partitioning (RPART), Bagging, and Adaptive Boosting.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: Random Forest achieved the highest overall performance with an Accuracy of 0.901, Kappa of 0.801, Sensitivity of 0.980, Specificity of 0.815, and AUC of 0.966.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: Global Feature Importance (Variable importance was evaluated using Mean Decrease in Accuracy and Mean Decrease in Gini Index). No localized XAI tools like SHAP or LIME were used.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided directly to students.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. However, the study proposes policy-level system features: establishing a central data analytics hub for the ASEAN University Network (AUN), utilizing mHealth apps to rapidly collect the top 5 salient features (BMI, sports, GPA, sedentary hours, age) to shorten survey times, and creating a digital dashboard for active monitoring by university stakeholders.
Main_Strengths: Exceptionally large, multi-national sample size representing the Southeast Asian (ASEAN) region; robust comparison of multiple machine learning classifiers; successfully identifies a concise, practical set of easily measurable behavioral features to predict mental well-being.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences; relies entirely on self-reported survey data, making it vulnerable to reporting bias; binary classification of mental well-being may oversimplify complex psychological states.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Total absence of objective, passive digital logging or continuous physiological data (the authors explicitly suggest future models incorporate biofeedback such as EEG, ECG, and heart rate); lack of individualized explainable AI (XAI) techniques to provide transparent local predictions; need for longitudinal data to track mental health trajectories.

Authors_and_Year: Mohammad Rezaur Rahman, Sayma Sharmen, Morshed Alam (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Undergraduate private university students | Dhaka, Bangladesh
Primary_Objective: To investigate the influence of Self-Evaluation Traits (SET) and Career Decision-Making Difficulties (CDMD) on student burnout, and to examine the mediating role of Social Support (SS) utilizing the Conservation of Resources (COR) theory.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS) (used to measure emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and diminished accomplishment).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 5-point Likert scale surveys measuring: Self-Evaluation Traits (12 items), Career Decision-Making Difficulties (8 items), Social Support (12 items), and Student Burnout (9 items). Demographic factors included gender, age, field of study, and year of study.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study employed traditional statistical modeling, specifically Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via Smart PLS-4 and IBM SPSS.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The PLS-SEM path model demonstrated adequate predictive relevance and fit, explaining 26.6% of the variance in Student Burnout (R² = 0.266).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Relies on traditional white-box PLS-SEM path coefficients and mediation analysis).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study provides institutional policy recommendations, emphasizing the need for twofold interventions: (1) building organized social support networks (peer mentoring, faculty engagement) to mitigate situational career-decision stress, and (2) implementing self-efficacy training to maintain internal resilience.
Main_Strengths: Successfully addresses a major geographical gap by focusing on an LMIC context (private university students in Bangladesh); clarifies the distinct roles of internal resources (SET) versus external situational factors (CDMD) in predicting burnout; employs robust PLS-SEM methodology including common method bias and collinearity checks.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions; convenience sampling restricted to a single city (Dhaka) limits broader national or international generalizability.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete reliance on self-report questionnaires with no integration of objective behavioral markers or passive digital logging; absence of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models and explainable AI (XAI) frameworks; lacks longitudinal tracking to validate the suggested interventions over time.

Authors_and_Year: Yanling Lan, Sihang Liu, Hao Chen (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: College students | Fujian Province, China
Primary_Objective: To examine the psychological pathways linking AI affordances (perceived usefulness, inert thinking, perceived enjoyment) to learning burnout, utilizing a serial mediation model based on the I-PACE framework (AI dependence -> AI addiction).
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Learning Burnout (LB) scale (adapted from Schaufeli et al., 2002; essentially derived from the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Likert-scale surveys assessing: Perceived Usefulness of AI, Inert Thinking, Perceived Enjoyment, AI Dependence, AI Addiction, and Learning Burnout. Demographic factors included gender, academic qualification, and major.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study relied entirely on traditional statistical modeling, specifically Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) executed via SmartPLS and SPSS.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The PLS-SEM path model successfully validated the serial mediation hypotheses (e.g., perceived usefulness → AI dependence → AI addiction → learning burnout). Model adequacy was verified with SRMR (0.082) and NFI (0.807).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Interpretability relies on standard white-box structural equation path coefficients and mediation analysis).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not a technological intervention system. The study recommends institutional and curricular interventions, including: developing "AI conscious learning modules" to train metacognitive regulation, fostering "Creative Engagement" teaching methods to counter inert thinking, and establishing an "AI Behavior Supervision and Healthy Use System" to track student learning data and provide behavioral feedback.
Main_Strengths: Innovatively applies the established I-PACE (Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution) addiction framework to the modern context of generative AI; clearly defines the mechanistic progression from instrumental AI reliance to pathological AI addiction and subsequent burnout.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents definitive causal inference of the sequential pathways; the sample is limited to a single province in China (Fujian), constraining generalizability; reliance on a unidirectional structural model ignores potential cyclical feedback loops between burnout and addiction.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete absence of objective behavioral data, such as passive digital logging of actual AI tool usage (e.g., screen time, prompt frequency); lack of longitudinal studies to track the temporal evolution of AI addiction; absence of predictive Machine Learning models or XAI frameworks; lack of cross-cultural validation, particularly in other LMICs like Bangladesh.

Authors_and_Year: Wasit Wongtrakul, Yodying Dangprapai, Nattha Saisavoey, Naratip Sa-nguanpanich (2023)
Target_Population_and_Region: Preclinical medical students | Bangkok, Thailand
Primary_Objective: To culturally adapt, translate, and validate the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBI-SS) for use in a Thai context among preclinical medical students.

ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study relied on traditional inferential statistics, specifically multiple linear regression models, Mann-Whitney U tests, Kruskal-Wallis H tests, and Spearman’s Rho.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The multiple linear regression models accounted for modest variances in the burnout subscales: 10.5% for Emotional Exhaustion (EE), 5.8% for Lack of Personal Accomplishment (LPA), and 10.2% for Depersonalization (DP). Notably, being female was a strong predictor of EE, while male gender and paid employment predicted higher DP.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Interpretability relies on standard white-box regression coefficients).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study recommends institutional and curricular strategies, such as: (1) strengthening professional exposure and coping tools during pre-clinical years (years 1-3) to prepare students for the clinical transition in year 4; (2) providing targeted support to compensate for educational disadvantages based on high school background; and (3) employing gender-specific psychological interventions, given that men tend to evade (DP) while women experience emotional depletion (EE).
Main_Strengths: Large sample size covering a diverse range of health science programs, not just medical students (e.g., Speech Therapy, Pharmaceutical Chemistry); effectively highlights the highly gendered and program-specific manifestations of burnout (EE vs. DP).
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents the establishment of causality; non-probabilistic quota sampling method and restriction to a single university in Chile limit broad generalizability.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete reliance on a self-administered questionnaire without any objective behavioral indicators or passive digital logging; absence of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models and Explainable AI (XAI) to track burnout trajectories; while it provides data from a Latin American context, it lacks cross-regional applicability to other LMICs like Bangladesh.

Authors_and_Year: Nils Olson, Renate Oberhoffer-Fritz, Barbara Reiner, Thorsten Schulz (2025)

Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Sociodemographic factors (age, gender), academic faculty affiliation, number of semesters studied, self-reported academic workload (weekly hours), occupational working hours (side-jobs), and study satisfaction.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study employed traditional inferential statistics, specifically Analysis of Variance (ANOVA/Welch-ANOVA), pairwise comparisons (Tukey's test), and binary logistic regression using SPSS.

For example, higher study satisfaction significantly reduced the odds of emotional exhaustion (OR = 0.702), while increased academic workload slightly increased the odds of cynicism (OR = 1.013) but also increased study engagement (OR = 1.014).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Interpretability relies on standard white-box logistic regression Odds Ratios).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.

Authors_and_Year: Yuhei Hara, Shota Furuta, Ayako Sukegawa, Koichiro Fujimaki, Shinya Hisano (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: Students (Elementary school through University) | Global (Systematic Review)
Primary_Objective: To systematically identify and evaluate the methodological quality and psychometric properties of existing self-report instruments used to measure student burnout, utilizing the rigorous COSMIN guidelines.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: The study evaluated 33 tools, prominently including various adaptations of the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI-SS), the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT-C, S-BAT), the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI-S), and the School Burnout Inventory (SBI).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: The study evaluated the structural validity, internal consistency, content validity, cross-cultural validity, and measurement invariance of the self-reported survey instruments themselves.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. This was a systematic review of psychometric tools evaluating measurement properties using the COSMIN risk-of-bias checklist.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: None / Not Applicable. Strikingly, the review found that exactly ZERO (0) instruments currently meet the COSMIN criteria to be recommended for use, primarily due to inadequate content validity.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study makes a strong methodological recommendation: researchers must stop relying on occupational burnout adaptations (like the MBI-SS) and urgently prioritize the de novo development of student-specific burnout measures. This must begin with rigorous content validity studies involving in-depth qualitative interviews with students to accurately capture their lived experiences.
Main_Strengths: Highly rigorous methodology adhering strictly to PRISMA and COSMIN guidelines; exposes a massive foundational flaw in current student burnout research (the lack of valid measurement tools); highlights that newer tools (like BAT-C) have superior structural validity compared to older tools (MBI).
Key_Limitations: The review excluded non-English publications, which likely excluded valid instruments from other linguistic and cultural contexts; potential publication bias where studies showing poor psychometric properties are not published; the reviewers lacked specialized formal training in COSMIN application.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: The review identifies a complete absence of data on "responsiveness" and "measurement error" in existing tools, severely limiting their use in longitudinal tracking or intervention testing. Furthermore, as a review of psychological surveys, it highlights the field's total reliance on subjective self-reporting, emphasizing the unaddressed gap of using objective, passive digital logging to measure burnout. It also lacks any integration of predictive Machine Learning (ML) or Explainable AI (XAI), and by excluding non-English studies, it likely underrepresents LMIC contexts (e.g., Bangladesh).

Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Self-reported GenAI dependency across three dimensions: Affect (e.g., anxiety/uneasiness when AI is unavailable), Cognition (e.g., belief that AI-generated code is superior to own code), and Behavior (e.g., unconsciously turning to AI even for simple tasks). Demographic variables included gender and birthplace (urban/rural).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study relied on traditional psychometric scale development techniques, including Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) using SPSS and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) using the CB-SEM module in SmartPLS.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The proposed 3-factor CFA model demonstrated a good fit to the data (RMSEA = 0.070, CFI = 0.981, TLI = 0.976), significantly outperforming a unidimensional 1-factor model. The scale also exhibited strong internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.963).

Main_Strengths: Addresses a highly contemporary educational challenge (GenAI dependence vs. addiction) with a domain-specific tool tailored specifically for programming students; utilizes a large sample size (N=1,295); strongly grounded in the theoretical ABC (Affect, Behavior, Cognition) framework.
Key_Limitations: Test-retest reliability was not assessed, leaving the temporal stability of the scale unverified; initial scale items were generated from interviews with instructors rather than the students themselves; convenience sampling via WeChat/QQ groups may limit representativeness.

Authors_and_Year: Rasikh Tariq, M. G. Orozco-del-Castillo, Muhammad Tayyab Zamir, Maria Soledad Ramírez-Montoya, Tabbi Wilberforce (2025)
Target_Population_and_Region: University students | Mexico
Primary_Objective: To develop a cost-effective, survey-based machine learning classification model for student stress detection, utilizing eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to ensure transparent and actionable institutional decision-making.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: A custom survey predicting discrete stress levels (0 = low, 1 = medium, 2 = high).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: 21 features spanning five domains: Psychological (anxiety level, self-esteem, mental health history, depression), Physiological (headache, blood pressure, sleep quality, breathing problems), Social (peer pressure, teacher-student relationship, extracurricular activities, social support, bullying), Environmental (noise level, living conditions, safety, basic needs), and Academic (academic performance, study load, future career concerns).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: Random Forest achieved the most balanced high performance with an Accuracy of 0.88, Precision of 0.88, Recall of 0.88, and F1-Score of 0.88. Logistic Regression and SVM also performed comparably well (Accuracy = 0.89).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and traditional Feature Importance plots were heavily utilized to unpack the "black-box" models. Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.

The study recommends using the XAI insights to drive institutional policy changes, specifically: implementing campus health monitoring (focusing on sleep hygiene and blood pressure), improving campus safety protocols, funding extracurricular clubs to build social networks, and training faculty in relational pedagogy to improve teacher-student dynamics.
Main_Strengths: Superb use of modern Explainable AI (SHAP) to interpret ML models, allowing for targeted policy recommendations; utilizes a highly multidimensional dataset (21 features across 5 life domains).
Key_Limitations: The article has been formally retracted. Additionally, it relies on self-reported physiological markers (e.g., asking students to self-report their blood pressure), which lacks clinical validity compared to actual sensor data; cross-sectional design prevents causal tracking.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Despite its data-driven approach, it completely lacks objective, passive digital logging (e.g., smartphone usage or wearable sensor data), relying entirely on subjective self-report questionnaires. Authors_and_Year: Chao Jin, Wen Long, Linna Wang, Zhikang Liu, Liangliang Sun (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: College students | Shandong Province, China
Primary_Objective: To explore the structural relationship between mobile phone addiction and academic burnout, specifically investigating the mediating role of learning engagement and the moderating role of physical exercise.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Maslach Burnout Inventory-Student Survey (MBISS) (Chinese revised version, assessing emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and inefficacy).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Mobile phone addiction (Mobile Phone Dependence Index Scale - MPDIS), learning engagement (Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-Student - UWES-S), academic burnout (MBISS), and physical exercise volume (Physical Exercise Rating Scale - PARS-3). Demographic covariates included gender and grade.
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: None. The study relied on traditional statistical modeling, utilizing the PROCESS macro (Models 4 and 7) in SPSS for mediation and moderated mediation analyses.
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The moderated mediation model demonstrated that mobile phone addiction positively predicts academic burnout. Learning engagement acts as a significant mediator, accounting for 20.7% of the total effect. Furthermore, physical exercise acts as a significant moderator; high levels of physical exercise effectively neutralize the negative impact of mobile phone addiction on learning engagement.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Interpretability relies on standard white-box regression coefficients and mediation/moderation effect sizes).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study provides structural recommendations: universities should implement digital well-being education focusing on cognitive-behavioral self-regulation, enhance campus network management, and strictly enforce physical fitness programs to help students restore cognitive resources depleted by excessive mobile phone use.
Main_Strengths: Successfully integrates physical activity as a protective moderating variable against the cognitive depletion caused by mobile phone addiction; utilizes a robust moderated mediation statistical framework grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory.
Key_Limitations: The cross-sectional design precludes establishing definitive causality; data collected from a single province limits national and international generalizability; reliance on self-report questionnaires exposes the findings to social desirability bias (e.g., overreporting exercise or underreporting phone addiction).
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete absence of objective behavioral data—such as passive digital logging of actual smartphone screen time or objective wearable data for physical exercise tracking; absence of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models or Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks; lacks cross-cultural validation in LMICs outside of China, such as Bangladesh.

Authors_and_Year: Mst. Nilufar Yasmin, Mohammad Mizanur Rahman, Nusrat Y. Ahmed, Amrin Binte Ahmed, Adisha Dulmini, Muhammad Khairul Alam, Atikur Rahman, Rumana Rois (2026)
Target_Population_and_Region: University students | Bangladesh
Primary_Objective: To apply an exploratory, explainable machine learning framework to analyze and predict complex patterns of depression, anxiety, and stress among university students in Bangladesh during a period of significant social unrest.
Burnout_Mental_Health_Tool: Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale (DASS-21) and the Internet Addiction Test (IAT).
Self_Reported_Survey_Indicators: Psychological outcomes (DASS-21), Internet Addiction (IAT), demographic data (gender, university type, academic discipline, BMI), and behavioral/psychosocial variables (e.g., waking up from bad dreams, memory loss symptoms, misbehavior, smoking status, religious activity, Google Classroom usage).
ML_Algorithms_Evaluated: Decision Trees (DT), Random Forests (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Logistic Regression (LR), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN).
Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The overall predictive performance was relatively modest due to the highly skewed, high-symptom sample. Support Vector Machine (SVM) demonstrated the most stable performance for predicting Depression (Accuracy = 0.696, F1 = 0.787) and Stress (Accuracy = 0.660, F1 = 0.688). XGBoost was selected for Anxiety (Accuracy = 0.715, F1 = 0.819) due to a better balance of sensitivity and specificity.
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: Highly rigorous use of XAI. Utilized the Boruta algorithm for feature selection, followed by SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) for global feature importance and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) for local, individual-level prediction transparency. Sankey diagrams were also used to visualize feature-outcome associations.
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The authors explicitly state that their explainable ML framework is an exploratory, hypothesis-generating tool for pattern recognition. Because the models largely leveraged overlapping symptomatology (e.g., using "bad dreams" to predict "depression") rather than independent antecedent risk factors, they strongly advise against deploying this specific model as a clinical screening tool.
Main_Strengths: Addresses a massive geographical gap by conducting an advanced ML/XAI study specifically in Bangladesh (an LMIC); utilizes state-of-the-art explainability techniques (SHAP and LIME) to demystify black-box ML models; demonstrates acute awareness of the tautological risks in using self-reported symptoms to predict other self-reported symptoms.
Key_Limitations: Non-probability purposive online sampling during a period of extreme national political unrest (July 2024 student protests) resulted in a highly skewed sample with exceptionally high distress prevalence (e.g., 73.4% severe anxiety), limiting generalizability; cross-sectional design prevents causal inference.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete absence of objective behavioral data or passive digital logging. Despite assessing variables like Internet Addiction, sleep quality, and BMI, all data was entirely self-reported. The authors explicitly call for future research to utilize longitudinal tracking to establish temporal inference, which passive sensing could facilitate.

Authors_and_Year: Munassir Alhamami, Abdulaziz Alrabai (2026)

Best_Performing_Model_and_Metrics: The PLS-SEM measurement model demonstrated excellent convergent and discriminant validity (all AVEs > 0.81). The structural model revealed that Exhaustion had the strongest path coefficient (0.955) to overall burnout and the highest predictive relevance (Q²predict = 0.912) and lowest error (RMSE = 0.299).
XAI_Interpretability_Techniques: None / Not Applicable. (Interpretability relies on standard white-box PLS-SEM path coefficients, R² values, and Q²predict metrics).
Personalized_Recommendations: No algorithmic personalized recommendations were provided.
Actionable_System_Features: Not an actionable technological system. The study recommends structural educational interventions tailored to EMI students: implementing targeted language support (e.g., continuous proficiency workshops), adopting inclusive teaching strategies (e.g., visual aids, glossaries to lower cognitive load), and embedding mental health resources directly into EMI program structures.
Main_Strengths: Successfully addresses a unique, high-stress subpopulation (students learning complex material in a second language); develops a highly contextualized psychometric tool; utilizes robust structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to validate the scale.
Key_Limitations: The scale was validated exclusively in Saudi Arabia, meaning its stability in other cultural or linguistic settings is untested; the cross-sectional design prevents assessing the temporal development of burnout; the study did not test for measurement invariance across gender or disciplines.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Relies entirely on self-report questionnaires, missing the opportunity to integrate objective behavioral data via passive digital logging (e.g., tracking late-night LMS activity or assignment writing dynamics to corroborate exhaustion); complete absence of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models or Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks; lacks cross-cultural validation in LMICs outside the Middle East, such as Bangladesh.

The study provides structural recommendations for academic institutions: rebuilding academic confidence through constructive feedback and mentoring programs; prioritizing accessible mental health services (counseling and therapy); and actively encouraging healthy social connections (e.g., student clubs) to combat the isolation frequently experienced by international students.
Main_Strengths: Focuses on a unique subpopulation (international students studying abroad) facing distinct cross-cultural adaptation stressors; explicitly differentiates between the constructs of chronic burnout and general anxiety.
Key_Limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents the establishment of causal relationships; the sample size is relatively small and drawn from a single college in Croatia, limiting broad generalizability; the study utilized the occupational MBI rather than the student-specific MBI-SS, which the authors justify but remains a methodological limitation.
Unaddressed_Research_Gaps: Complete reliance on subjective self-report questionnaires, which the authors acknowledge could lead to inflated perceptions of burnout. There is a total absence of objective behavioral data or passive digital logging to corroborate these high stress levels; lack of predictive Machine Learning (ML) models or Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks; geographically centered in an upper-middle-income EU country (Croatia), leaving gaps regarding LMICs such as Bangladesh.
